summary:
No Hidalgo-specific statute, enforcement pattern or documented incident affecting trans people is supported by the vetted sources for this record. The operative framework is Mexico's national one, in which legal gender recognition is legislated state by state.

As of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had enacted an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Two further states operate such a procedure in practice without having legislated it, six state legislatures have enacted nothing, and only seven states extend recognition to children.

Where a state has no procedure, the consequence documented by Human Rights Watch is identity-document mismatch that drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market; incidents of that kind were recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

The Supreme Court of Mexico set binding guidelines for the states on recognition in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, while the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. A trans visitor in Hidalgo therefore stands under national and supranational doctrine even where state-level machinery is absent.

For a visitor, Hidalgo's own documented record is thin. Expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protection or verified local hostility.
tangentialFactors:
The effect of a silent state law is set out in detail by Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion in their 6 March 2024 report on Tabasco, a state with no recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are shut out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

That report was written against a backdrop of lethal violence and impunity: the murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa in August 2023, and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022.

Violence continued into 2024. AP reported in January of that year that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has closed a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe it as critical to their sense of safety.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice. The analysis cautions that it must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
localsOnly:
Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states on legal gender recognition in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, so residents can invoke national doctrine before state authorities regardless of local legislation.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple and accessible recognition procedure, giving residents a further avenue beyond domestic administration.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

Only seven states extend legal gender recognition to children, leaving a gap for families with trans minors that adult procedures do not close.

Residents of the two states identified as running a procedure without enactment rely on administrative practice rather than statute, which leaves that route vulnerable to change without a legislative vote.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Hidalgo Congress has enacted an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure is not stated in the sources reviewed for this record. The record establishes neither a local protection nor a local prohibition.

The six state legislatures counted by Human Rights Watch as having enacted no procedure are not named in the source, so Hidalgo's position within the national mosaic cannot be assigned from this material. This remains unresolved.

No Hidalgo-specific incident, police stop, document-refusal, hospital or ID-office policy, or state court decision appears in the inventory. Verification would require Hidalgo state gazette records and local reporting, which are not sourced here.

The record does not establish which agency in Hidalgo would receive a recognition request, what fees or timelines apply, or whether any municipal identity programme operates in the state. These points are unsourced rather than settled.
